title: It isn't too late
hookLine: after Karna, an old teacher pleads for peace, and Duryodhana says no
carry: it is never too late to turn toward dharma
tomorrow: who should face the new commander? not who you'd think.

cards: Karna is gone. Bhishma lies on his bed of arrows. Drona is dead.
The commanders Duryodhana trusted have fallen one after another, and in the Kaurava camp the king sits among the survivors, grieving. Then an old man speaks up.
It's Kripa, the teacher who trained these princes when they were boys, Kaurava and Pandava alike. He doesn't flatter. He tells the king the truth as he sees it.

teach.b: Kripa's counsel, in Ganguli's English, is plain: make peace with the Pandavas. Yudhishthira is gentle, he says in effect; he will still agree. There's still time.
And Duryodhana says no. His reasons are worth hearing. I've wronged them too deeply, he says; they'd never trust a peace from me now.
And my friends died for me. How could I live in comfort after sending them to die?
So Drona's son Ashvatthama names a new commander: Shalya, king of Madra, the man who drove Karna's chariot, and this book of the epic takes his name. Now the teaching.
Kripa's words are the Hindu answer, and Duryodhana's are the trap. It is never too late to turn toward dharma.

teach.h: THE GITA: TURN, AND YOU ARE COUNTED GOOD
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, spoken by Krishna on this same battlefield, he says that even someone of very bad conduct who turns to him with a whole heart is to be counted good, because he has resolved rightly.
Later retellings remember a forest robber who turned and became the sage Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana. Duryodhana's real enemy isn't the Pandava army.
It's the voice that says, I've gone too far to be trusted, so I may as well keep going.
The door Kripa held open was real. Duryodhana just couldn't believe it was open for him.

how: The Shalya Parva, the epic's book named for Shalya, is read and recited with the rest of the Mahabharata; Kripa's plea for peace and Duryodhana's refusal are retold as a turning point before the war's last day.

o: the old teacher who urges Duryodhana to make peace
the king of Madra who goes from Karna's driver to commander
Drona's son, who names the new Kaurava commander

games.q: the new command — tap the pairs.

s: after Karna died, nobody in the Kaurava camp spoke of peace
Kripa, the old teacher, urged Duryodhana to make peace.
Duryodhana refused because he thought he'd gone too far to be trusted
he didn't believe the Pandavas would accept a peace from him.
in the Gita, someone of very bad conduct is past saving
Krishna says even such a person, turning to him wholeheartedly, is to be counted good.

games.q: you said something cruel to a friend months ago and never fixed it. it feels too late now. by Kripa's counsel and the Gita, what fits?
o: reach out now; the turn is still open.
leave it; too much time has passed to be believed.
wait for them to bring it up first.
games.why: Duryodhana's 'too late to be trusted' kept the war going. Kripa and the Gita both say the door is still open.

practice: Sit tall. Bring to mind a road you've stayed on because turning back would mean admitting something. Kripa's point is that the turn is still open.
If you pray, offer that road to God in your own words, or with the name you use for God. If you don't pray, picture one small step back the way you came, and notice that it is still there to take.

wordCard.voice: Shalya. King of Madra, the twins' uncle, Karna's driver, and now the commander of the Kaurava army, after Duryodhana refuses peace.

orig.note: Shalya: king of Madra, Karna's charioteer, and the Kauravas' new commander.

carryVoice: Your line: it is never too late to turn toward dharma. Kripa said it, and Duryodhana couldn't hear it. That's day eight hundred forty-three.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, Kripa's counsel of peace, Duryodhana's refusal, and Shalya's appointment as commander on Ashvatthama's suggestion
Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Shalya's arrival intending to join the Pandavas and his being won over by Duryodhana
Bhagavad Gita 9.30–31 (even one of very bad conduct who worships with undivided devotion is to be regarded as good, for he has rightly resolved)
Valmiki as a robber turned sage, in later retellings (e.g., the Adhyatma Ramayana) and popular tradition; not told in the Valmiki Ramayana itself
